title: What are some good ways, films built up sympathy for apparently unlikeable characters?

commenti.body: The titular character of *Barry Lyndon* doesn't have a lot of redeeming qualities. He's a liar, a cheat, and an opportunist. He's impulsive, violent, entitled, careless, selfish, and terrible with money. From the outset, you know the film is about his inevitable downfall due to his many deficiencies and failures of character.  Yet I think most people sympathizing with him because he's pathetic to the point that one can't help but pity him, he's more annoying than evil, he exists in an unfair and ridiculous world, and a couple of times he performs actually noble or brave actions.

The sheriff in first blood

First he starts off as an asshole, and some of his team members follow his lead

then he watches those team members get picked off one by one and he breaks down in tears after he’s brutally threatened by Rambo with a knife to his throat

Later he tries to regain control and get to the place where Rambo is hiding but it’s too late - the situation is now completely out of his control and finally he ends up hiding and scared in his own police station - after he’s shot, he welcomes death as the town he swore to keep safe and boring is in flames and darkness all around him.  the stain of Vietnam is brought back home to America
 
at one point the sheriff’s own war medals are shown displayed behind his desk, and his lack of empathy for Vietnam veterans is his undoing 

When I was younger I thought he was just a straight asshole, but now I can see what he represents as a more complex character 

I feel like it’s a commentary on changing times and how we view the world differently as we age
I thought only one person died in Rambo. The guy killed by the rock?

Initially you find him naive but root for him anyway because he shows bravery yet is unfairly treated by both his lover and family, then you root for him because a lot of bad stuff happens to him, then you root for him because he finally found a way to get back at that treacherous society he lives in, even if it's by a dishonest way (he's still duelling people to improve his condition so he's braver than most) then, finally, you start thinking of him as an asshole when he seduces a woman for her money, but you don't feel too bad either because her husband is an unlikeable character and the wife prefers Redmond over him anyway. Then you root for him because he's a a good dad to his son, though you hate him for the way he treats his wife and his son in law but then you root for him because he loses his son until the ultimate showdown where you root for him because, not only his petty son in law tries to fight him when he's already depressed and dead inside, but he gracefully tries to make peace with his son in law, to no avail.

The movie oscillates between different feelings for the main character but it would be very hard to care for him if he wasn't somehow a better person than most of the rest of the characters in almost the entire duration of the movie. It's also part of the meaning of the movie, to show that no matter how morally upstanding a young man initially is, he will be worn down eventually by such an unjust society.

Of course Kubrick also has the poster child of this theme in Alexander DeLarge from ACO. You could also same the same idea is made with Humbert from Lolita. He really did like the duality of man huh? The Jungian thing, sir. Lol.

A few examples:

* Uncut Gems follows an absolute asshat around as he destroys his life. But somehow we still want that long shot bet to pay off.

* The Hurt Locker's main protagonist is kind of a douche. We respect him because he's good at disarming bombs -- but he puts his crew in danger, doesn't respect process and needlessly escalates shit by disrespecting his Sergeant. As we follow his character arc we realize he's addicted to it.

* Who’s Afraid of Virginia Woolf? has two completely unlikable characters yelling at each other for over two hours. The whole experience is an emotional roller coaster of "Oh, wait, that sucks. Poor folks. No, hang on, they're full of shit."

* Lilo & Stitch starts Stitch out as a 100% unlikable, destructive, alien super weapon. But Lilo sees him as a mirror of herself and because we care about Lilo she forces us to care about Stitch.

I think Anton Chigurh's character, though he's supposed to be a horrible serial killer, is presented in a way that makes him very likeable in a subtle way. 

Initially, he is shown as a mercyless crazy killer. The way he strangles a cop while smiling makes him unlikeable because we assume he's just sadistic.

Then there's a very important scene : he goes to a shop and talks with an old shopkeeper. Now, absolutely nobody in the audience wants that nice humble poor old salt-of-the-earth shopkeeper to die, and anton sort of plays with our expectations that he's going to kill him. But two things happen : one, we discover that Chigurh doesn't just kill people out of sadistic pleasure, he kills at random. When the old guy calls the coin, he wins, Chigurh spares his life. This may seem insignificant that a bad guy would kill people at random instead of for any other reason, but all of a sudden we discover he has an ethos and he abides by it, he's not just a monster. Also, it rules out other more petty motivations like greed, sexual pleasure, sadism, revenge. There's killings of innocents but it's nothing personal.

The second thing we discover in that scene is that Chigurh is funny. The way he trolls the old shopkeeper while also trolling the audience's expectation that he's going to kill him is a sure way to get an audience behind a character. A complicity builds up between us and him at that point, we know he's got no respect for anyone but he's got principles and anyone who will try to go against him will hit a brick wall. You cannot reason him, but you can win the coin flip so in a sense he's fair.

Then something else also subtle happens in later scenes : he gets injured and we see him apply first aid to himself. This is once again a small detail that may seem insignificant but it makes us feel empathy for his pain and yet he doesn't show much self-pity, because he fixes himself like a champ and that also makes him sympathetic. We don't like crybabies. It makes him somewhat inhuman too, but we like inhuman when it's badass inhuman.

After these scenes, you still think he's a scary character but you find yourself kinda rooting for him and enjoying it when he catches the smug cowboy guy or when he ultimately survives a car accident.

usually, when looking for reasons why we feel sympathy for a character, look for these :

Brave
Obsessional
Funny
Hard working (or principled, may not like what he does, but he does it anyway)
Unfairly wounded
Skilled
In danger
Loved by others
Kind hearted/innocent

You'll see that Chigurh actually check almost all of these boxes during the movie except maybe the two last ones (though the boys helping him at the end touches on the "loved by others" and the way he treats everyone the same speaks to a sort of alienated form of innocence).

As others have said, two common techniques are: (1) show us some of their good qualities, like bravery, resilience, cunning, and (2) show them suffering or failing to achieve their goals. Two other ways: (3) pit them against someone worse (Sidney Falco in Sweet Smell of Success is an oleaginous scumbag, but JJ is even worse), and (4) imo  centering the character as a protagonist just in itself gives us some sympathy for them, especially if there's not an opposing, sympathetic deuteragonist for us to identify with against them.

Each adaptation of *The Talented Mr. Ripley* (and the novel it's adapted from) attempts to make the audience sympathetic with a completely irredeemable monster. Never so far as to make you *like* him, or to side with him on an emotional level, but by placing the audience wholly inside his struggle to maintain his ruse, it starts relatively low on the criminal totem pole and works its way up gradually in its attempt to convince you to become at least somewhat invested in his getting away with crimes that the director fully expects you to have zero tolerance for at an intellectual level.

That’s skipping half the story though. Scorsese was supposed to direct it and had sat on the script for years. He knew it well because he was very involved with the earlier version of the script and had already moved on, not specifically because it was a clone of Taxi Driver or King Of Comedy.

The boys at the end show the opposite of the last two. They help, but then he gives one of them money and they begin to fight over it. He's a corruptive, poisonous influence, a symbol of and vector for the worst aspects of human nature.

Oh, that’s a great pick! Sgt. O'Neil is a classic example of a character who reveals complexities beneath his rough exterior. Building sympathy for unlikeable characters often involves showing their humanity in unexpected ways. Think about Nicholson in *As Good As It Gets*—Jack’s character is abrasive, ornery, and borderline insufferable. But then, there are those moments when you see his vulnerability and the genuine struggles he deals with. It’s impossible not to soften towards him once you understand what's beneath the surface. Films that succeed in this aspect usually allow their characters to display glimpses of kindness, moments of true struggle, or a hidden moral compass, giving the audience something to latch onto emotionally.

I think Scorsese is just fundamentally not interested in the superhero genre (which Joker tangentially is part of) - rightly or wrongly, he believes that it’s unsophisticated and not capable of expressing the same depth of thought and emotion as other genres. And so it’s very understandable that he would be disinterested in a Batman-related film that borrows liberally from his work. It’s like showing an artist a copy of a painting they did - they’re unlikely to be that impressed by it and would rather see something new. 

Scorsese has seen more films than any of us is ever likely to in our lifetime. He lives and breathes cinema, curates, preserves and promotes films from all over the world. He’s simply educated on a whole other level and so his tastes and standards are gonna be a lot different than the average person who watches movies as a casual hobby. And that’s fine, in fact it’s what makes him so special as a filmmaker, so I’m more than happy for him to not care about superhero movies.

Yeah but he moved on because he ultimately didn’t care about the Joker part of the story, he was only interested in the Arthur Fleck part. None of the connections to Batman interested him. I think he was trying to muster up the enthusiasm in himself but just couldn’t so he moved on.

* Abbas Kiarostami’s “Close Up” is an interesting example of this because the main character is actually a con artist who legitimately conned a family in the real life. The premise of “I pretended to be a famous director because I love movies” is ridiculous, something that could easily be dismissed as a motivation for a fictional character and dismissed as an easy lie for a desperate criminal in real life. In mixing the real and the fake so effectively, we can’t help but find sympathy for the fake Makhmalbaf and feel the love he has for the medium.

* “Paris, Texas” thrives on the central mystery of a man walking out of the desert, alone and mute, his absence and motivations a mystery. Slowly, in seeing Travis bond with his son and brother, we grow to like him, to seemingly gain a sense of him as a character, and that mystery, while unresolved, ceases to be a primary motivation as the relationship between the characters takes center-stage. >!Then, in a brilliant turn, we get the great ten-minute monologue at the heart of the story, where we learn just how abusive and neglectful Travis was. The tenderness and calm nature he shows through the film lead us to not only overlook the mystery, but assume he is a victim in some way. Instead, he’s a pathetic individual, a controlling abuser who abandons his son because he can’t face his actions. Whether or not Travis’ reuniting Hunter and Jane is the right choice fits the ambiguity of the film.!<

* “Sorcerer” begins with a long cold open where we see our principal characters commit all kinds of bastardry - murder, armed robbery, terrorism, fraud. But the environment and the work they endure is so punishing that, without much exposition or expressive monologues, you come to feel their desperation and root for them to somehow get out.
